⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker.
  • Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.
  • “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really rapidly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” stated Barker on Toolkit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-revealed third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

“I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really rapidly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” stated Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

“It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” said Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Recent findings suggest that barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” said Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

According to recent reports, “People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” mentioned Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

One of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how swiftly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

In a recent development, “I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” remarked Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

Directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

What Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, promptly says he fell short in “Obsession.”.

“Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

“Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” mentioned Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

Sources indicate that as Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

“I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that disney+ has some thematically deep sci-fi highlights, with a recent eight-part entry being a masterclass in exploring existential dread. Many of the best TV shows on Disney+ exist within the sci-fi genre, be it the likes of Alien: Earth or Andor. Both shows, Andor especially, took massive science fiction franchises and explored them in more nuanced ways than usual. While Star Wars does have some depth, Andor's exploration of war, rebellion, sexual assault, and many more thematically rich aspects proved it to be not only one of the best Star Wars TV shows, but one of Disney's best projects ever.

It has been revealed that easily, the show is among the best sci-fi series on Disney+, with another franchise taking a page out of Andor's book. That franchise is the Marvel Cinematic Universe, which has had a lengthy catalog of highlights released on the streaming service since 2021. The most recent of those was VisionQuest, which, while still working as an exciting, Easter egg-filled Marvel show full of fights, action sequences, and fun characters, emulated Andor by taking a popular franchise and diving deep into what makes it tick.

Recent findings suggest that in this sense, VisionQuest was a masterclass in exploring existential dread. The entire premise of the show centered on Vision, split between being the physical reincarnation of the hero who was rebuilt as a weapon and the loving synthezoid with memories from before Avengers: Infinity War, figuring out who he was, what that meant, and how to feel the emotions he once did. Existential dread often surrounds a lack of clarity on what humanity even is, which the entire quest was about for Vision.

This led to many extended scenes of Vision and his surrounding characters exploring humanity, emotions, and all of the things that make people what they are. More than any other Marvel series, and, indeed, other reveals of its genre on Disney+, VisionQuest put effort into exploring the soul of each and every character by making them confront what it meant to be a caring being, human or not. Across eight episodes, VisionQuest's excellent writing delivered a true masterclass.

These deeper themes may lead some to wonder why VisionQuest's post-credit scene was so intent on setting up Avengers: Doomsday, which, while likely to have depth of its own, is a big, event-style MCU movie. However, VisionQuest was actually perfect for this. VisionQuest's focus on lingering dread and finding connection in others seems to be central to Avengers: Doomsday, too. After all, Doom's vendetta seems linked to the parental relationships formed by the Avengers, and how the latter group is now living stolen lives, given that he lost his child.

A significant central pillar of VisionQuest was the relationship between Vision and Tommy Maximoff, his reincarnated son. Vision's connection to Tommy was instrumental in the former regaining his human emotions, while Avengers: Doomsday could explore Doom's lack of a child leading to his villainy. Moreover, the Vision family is key to the multiverse, especially with Wanda Maximoff being revived by Doom. Although VisionQuest's story is relatively self-contained, it seems as though it is a great thematic precursor to Avengers: Doomsday.

It has been revealed that when focusing less on VisionQuest's links to wider MCU aspects and looking at it as a conclusion of the WandaVision trilogy, it becomes clear that this is the gold standard of Marvel Television. WandaVision, Agatha All Along, and VisionQuest are all incredibly unique, from the former's sitcom format and the latter's visual representation of AI thought processes to Agatha All Along's gothic Witches' Road setting. This allows each one to shine as its own thing, rather than a mere product of an oversaturated genre.

Moreover, to match the creativity on display, all three indicates are excellently written. Each tells its own story with its own unique cast of characters, while still linking together as a trilogy. More than anything else on Disney+, VisionQuest and its prequels shine as a perfect trilogy, with the show in question providing a masterclass in the exploration of existential dread.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before Robert Downey Jr. spent more than a decade saving the Marvel Cinematic Universe as Iron Man, he was busy reinventing another rather famous character. Bare knuckle brawling, intrepid investigating, slow motion violence, wit, women, wonder — Downey brought it all to the table.

Guy Ritchie's Sherlock Holmes movies turned Arthur Conan Doyle's legendary detective into an action hero who could solve a murder and beat up half the room without breaking a sweat. The first movie was a hit, and its sequel went even bigger, sending Holmes and Watson across Europe to face their most dangerous enemy yet. Fifteen years later, there's still no third movie, but fans can at least revisit the last adventure.

It has been revealed that ritchie's Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows has officially joined HBO Max's streaming library in the United States, having arrived on November 1, 2026. There is a new criminal mastermind at large, Professor Moriarty, and not only is he Holmes' intellectual equal, but his capacity for evil, coupled with a complete lack of conscience, may actually give him an advantage over the renowned detective. When the Crown Prince of Austria is found dead, the evidence, as construed by Inspector Lestrade points to suicide. But Sherlock Holmes deduces that the prince has been the victim of a murder that is only one piece of a larger and much more portentous puzzle, designed by one Professor Moriarty.

Released in December 2011, A Game of Shadows earned approximately $543.8 million worldwide against a reported $125 million budget, following the success of the original Sherlock Holmes in 2009.

The cast includes Downey Jr. (Avengers: Doomsday) as Sherlock Holmes, Jude Law (The Talented Mr. Ripley) as Dr. John Watson, Noomi Rapace (The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo) as Simza Heron, Jared Harris (Chernobyl) as Professor James Moriarty, Rachel McAdams (Mean Girls) as Irene Adler, Stephen Fry (The Hobbit) as Mycroft Holmes, Kelly Reilly (Yellowstone) as Mary Watson, and Eddie Marsan (Ray Donovan) as Inspector Lestrade.

Ritchie has since returned to Conan Doyle's characters with Young Sherlock, starring Hero Fiennes Tiffin as a younger version of the detective. Meanwhile, a third movie starring Downey Jr. and Law has spent years in development without reaching production.

Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows is streaming now on HBO Max in the United States.

#108581. Star Wars’ 2-Part Sci-Fi War Thriller Has One of the Best Seasons in TV History

Star Wars’ 2-Part Sci-Fi War Thriller Has One of the Best Seasons in TV History

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in 2022, Disney was having a pretty strange year with its franchises.
  • In a recent development, however, some franchises fared much worse with their fans than others.
  • Industry observers note that those fans were wrong.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in 2022, Disney was having a pretty strange year with its franchises. There were some major wins, such as the hugely financially successful release of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness and Turning Red becoming a streaming hit. Its films also earned $4.9 billion at the box office that year.

In a recent development, however, some franchises fared much worse with their fans than others. After the poor reception of The Book of Boba Fett in February and the controversy surrounding Obi-Wan Kenobi in May, Star Wars fans weren't particularly hopeful that Andor, Tony Gilroy’s gritty spy series, would restore the franchise to its former greatness.

Industry observers note that those fans were wrong. Gilroy didn’t just renew fans' hope that Star Wars could be more than a franchise for children; he delivered a culturally relevant story about the sacrifices people make — love, comfort, and friendship — in the fight against tyranny, all within a single season. The series also expanded the background of a beloved character, Cassian Andor, so that even if a second season had never arrived, that story would have worked perfectly as a sequel to Star Wars' most beloved films.

It has been revealed that though Andor’s second season is more critically acclaimed — and has a handful of awards under its belt — its 12-episode first season is immaculate at showcasing how the Empire’s oppressive grip destroys the hope of those living under its regime. It also kickstarts Cassian Andor’s ascent into the hardcore rebel fans know from Rogue One.

According to recent reports, the series opens with Cassian (Diego Luna) searching for his sister on Morlana One, where he runs into trouble and kills two Pre-Mor security officers. On the run, he returns home to the planet Ferrix and tries to sell an Imperial Starpath unit to fund his escape, but he gets caught up in the machinations of the rebel organization known as the Axis Network, led by Luthen Rael (Stellan Skarsgård).

A survivalist first and foremost, Cassian is staunchly opposed to getting caught up in the rebellion against the Empire — right up until he can no longer look away from the Imperial machine and the horrors it inflicts.

Recent findings suggest that star Wars has always been a story about a group of revolutionaries fighting a tyrannical empire, but most of the audience’s time has been spent following major-shot heroes and chosen ones like Han Solo, Leia Organa, and Luke Skywalker. There were always Jedi, and the good guys rarely, if ever, lost.

That isn’t the case for Andor, which, like its predecessor Rogue One, follows the little guys — the people who aren’t showered with public praise and given medals as rewards. Even in the brief time we spend with minor characters like the insurgents on Aldhani and the prisoners of Narkina-5, each is given complexity and a compelling reason to fight the Empire. No one is driven by the Force or has a secret, epic backstory. They're on the ground fighting for what they believe in, or in most cases, because they have no other choice.

In a recent development, it helps that Andor is possibly the most beautiful Star Wars has ever looked on television. From Aldhani’s cultural event in the Scottish Highlands — one of Star Wars’ most heart-stopping moments — to Ferrix, built brick by brick, Gilroy’s production values are unmatched. It doesn’t just look like a Star Wars show’s backdrop. Each planet feels lived-in, with communities that feel unique in both appearance and behavior.

Andor season 1 is Star Wars at its very best: an epic, winding tale of Cassian’s journey from thief and scoundrel to a man who would inevitably sacrifice himself to give the Rebellion those all-vital Death Star prepares. The people he meets along the way, from Mon Mothma to Luthen Rael, are equally brilliant at showing how far people will go to bloody the nose of the Imperial machine.

Andor’s second season is every bit as compelling as the first, with each trio of episodes in the 12-episode season spanning a year. Still, Gilroy’s original five-season plan being cut to two is evident in the leaps in character development between episodes, leaving some choices unearned and, frankly, at odds with what audiences see in Rogue One. It is still leagues above many Star Wars highlights — though Rebels will always remain my favorite — but compared to how tightly contained season 1 is in telling Cassian Andor's story, season 2 just doesn’t compare to the masterpiece that is the debut season.

How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • World-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

World-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he says he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he remarked through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Recent findings suggest that but he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I said, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

According to recent reports, at the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he mentioned. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

In a recent development, his 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” stated Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

Industry observers note that how’s his French? “Zero,” he remarked. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

The filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” noted Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

When it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” noted Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

One serious issue for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he said. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

Of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he stated. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

The filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

It has been revealed that and Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he mentioned. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

It has been revealed that was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he said. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he stated, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alien: Isolation 2 is a rare treat that would’ve been difficult to predict.
  • According to recent reports, alien: Isolation 2 had a playable demo featured at Gamescom in August, and it may not be much longer before the game is fully released.
  • Alien: Isolation 2 has massive moon boots to fill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alien: Isolation 2 is a rare treat that would’ve been difficult to predict. Indeed, the fact that Alien: Isolation is receiving a sequel more than a decade later is a testament to how profoundly influential it’s been for the horror genre. There’s no doubt that the Alien/Aliens franchise is well-established in horror, but Alien: Isolation is arguably the one Alien video game to most faithfully and authentically represent that horror.

According to recent reports, alien: Isolation 2 had a playable demo featured at Gamescom in August, and it may not be much longer before the game is fully released. Regardless, thanks to how many heavy hitters it could boast, 2027 is rapidly taking shape as one of the best years for horror games in a while.

Alien: Isolation 2 has massive moon boots to fill. It’ll be neat to see whether stealth has been significantly improved, for instance, and whether the sequel is as long as its predecessor (one of the biggest critiques of Alien: Isolation to this day being that it’s exceedingly long).

Sources indicate that as to whether or not Alien: Isolation 2 will have a physical edition, Creative Assembly’s response in a Dev Q&A video was incredibly encouraging: “Staying true to the analogue nature of Alien is one of our core pillars. Alien: Isolation 2 will have a physical edition.” This guarantees that the studio is at least eyeing a 2027 release window, considering that PlayStation’s shift toward an all-digital future goes into full effect in early 2028, though it’s possible that it’ll only have physical editions for the consoles that accommodate it by the time it actually introduces.

In a recent development, assuming that Alien: Isolation 2 isn’t delayed, this highly anticipated sequel could be horror’s crown jewel in 2027. 12 years after the launch of the first game, 2027 will be a celebration of the stealth-oriented, first-person-perspective horror games that Alien: Isolation and its ilk directly inspired, as well as other unique horror games in general.

Launching in 2027 are The Lost Wild, a dinosaur survival horror game whose game director was Alien: Isolation’s lead designer, and Ontos, a psychological horror game from Amnesia: The Dark Descent and Soma’s Frictional Games. Both are horror. Plus, there are plenty of indie horror games that may not already be on your radar, such as the low-poly Resident Evil and Dark Souls-esque game False Oath.

Of course, Resident Evil Veronica being slated for 2027 ensures that the year will be thrilling nonetheless. Resident Evil Veronica ironically has the lightest weight on its shoulders of any Resident Evil remake to come before it (let alone any remake that follows it). That remarked, Resident Evil Veronica is much more of a black sheep and may not have as many fans in its corner as the Resident Evil 4 remake or Resident Evil Requiem did, perhaps because Resident Evil Code: Veronica is likely the mainline entry that the fewest fans have played.

In a recent development, beginning with the launch of the Silent Hill 2 remake, Silent Hill has given itself the unenviable task of releasing a new game every year—Silent Hill 2’s remake in 2024, Silent Hill f in 2025, and Silent Hill: Townfall in 2026. There hasn’t been any confirmation regarding whether or not Bloober’s Silent Hill 1 remake will launch in 2027, but it would certainly align with the franchise’s newfound annual release schedule.

It’d be sad if Silent Hill misses out on such a fantastic year for horror, especially when the series’ installments have been fairly great lately. Moreover, fans can look forward to ILL and Until Dawn 2, with Until Dawn 2 being particularly exciting for anyone who adored the original Until Dawn and feels as though Supermassive’s choice-driven games still haven’t exceeded its golden standard. Either way, 2027 will be dominated by the horror genre, and Alien: Isolation 2 would be the icing on its cake.

Long-awaited sequel to 2014's survival horror classic Alien: Isolation.

'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (482 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • Recent findings suggest that as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's notable to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

Recent findings suggest that as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that tech giant or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

Next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, upgrade the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In the age of the streaming wars, Netflix's response to Paramount+'s British-laden MobLand is yet another English-centric crime drama, The Gentlemen.
  • The reception for the first two seasons of The Gentlemen has been widely positive by critics, with Netflix also enjoying viewership success.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Organized crime has been an issue for every single civilization that has ever existed. The 2010s seemed like the golden age of crime dramas, with demonstrates like Boardwalk Empire starring Steve Buscemi, Narcos, Ozark, and Netflix's hit crime series, Peaky Blinders, starring Cillian Murphy, among several bingeworthy treats on offer. Thankfully, the 2020s have not disappointed. While the legacy of Tommy Shelby lives on beyond the events of Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man in its upcoming sequel series. Other organized crime dramas have since come on the scene. Gangs of London, Paramount+'s two-pronged delight in Tulsa King and MobLand are some of the sub-genre's more glittering additions in recent years.

In the age of the streaming wars, Netflix's response to Paramount+'s British-laden MobLand is yet another English-centric crime drama, The Gentlemen. The hugely ambitious producer, creator, and filmmaker, Guy Ritchie, is the firm bond that links both shows together, as Ritchie serves in several capacities behind the scenes for both productions. The second season of the Netflix series recently wrapped, signaling the initiation of production on Season 3, which is already underway. As is to be expected, several fresh cast additions and departures will be associated with the new chapter, even as its main stars, Theo James as the central crime boss, Edward "Eddie" Horniman, and Kaya Scodelario as Eddie's partner and associate, Sussie Glass.

The reception for the first two seasons of The Gentlemen has been widely positive by critics, with Netflix also enjoying viewership success. Hence, sights have turned to Season 3 and what it might bring. Speaking during a Q&A for Netflix's The Gentlemen Season 2 FYC screening earlier this month, executive producer Matthew Read and the show's cast teased some exciting story directions for Season 3. First off, Eddie and Susie are expanding the criminal empire into the Middle East, and it's a move Read describes as being "an ascension for Eddie and Susie to become bigger than ever" with Theo James drawing comparisons with Martin Scorsese and Robert De Niro's 1995 film Casino. "[Season 3] about expansion. It's about opening the first casino in the Middle East," Read explained to the attendance. "It's like Las Vegas, and that will involve lots of million-dollar deals. And there will be lots of people competing for the rights to run this casino. So it's a sort of elevation, and it's about ascension for Eddie and Susie to become bigger than ever." To all that, James adds, "If season 2 was The Godfather Part II, this is Casino.".

By the time the season finale of The Gentlemen Season 2 aired, it became clear that James' character, Edward Horniman, had fully embraced the darkness and his position within it as a mob boss in the criminal underworld. With the Italian mafia behind him, Eddie turns his sights to the Middle East and perhaps some of the contacts he secured during the Falcon mystery in Season 2 might begin to pay off. Heading forward into Season 3, his complicated relationship with Susie, and now this news of competition for control over the casino, sets the stage for yet another colossal tussle.

Filming for The Gentlemen Season 3 has production taking place in Morocco, presumably the set for the Middle East expansion, and more recently, around London. Alongside James and Scodelario, fresh faces will be arriving this coming season, including Orlando Bloom, Robert Carlyle, Elijah Wood, Ed Speleers, Bugzy Malone, Saffron Burrows, Bruna Marquezine, and Dexter Fletcher.

It has been revealed that the first two seasons of The Gentlemen are streaming on Netflix. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Season 3.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a upcoming popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler mentioned. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he said. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

More coverage from IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables will be published here over the coming weeks.

#108571. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2037 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger.
  • I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.
  • To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

It has been revealed that shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

It has been revealed that this major-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

Recent findings suggest that horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley highlights up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

According to recent reports, mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

Recent findings suggest that there's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

Recent findings suggest that I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

In a recent development, I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

It has been revealed that this BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

Industry observers note that the current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

2026 hasn't exactly been a banner year for Ridley Scott, who finally returned to the sci-fi genre after almost 10 years away to direct his newly introduced movie, The Dog Stars. Based on the critically acclaimed science fiction novel of the same name by Peter Heller, Scott even tapped Josh Brolin and Jacob Elordi to lead The Dog Stars, but that didn't translate to success at the box office.

In a recent development, the movie has since found success on VOD platforms like Prime Video and Apple TV after leaving theaters with one of the lowest-grossing box office totals of Scott's career. It won't take Scott long to seek redemption at the box office, either; he's returning to the screen in less than one year for a Treasure Island remake starring Hugh Jackman and Owen Cooper from the 2025 Netflix sensation, Adolescence.

Ridley Scott is on something of a cold streak right now after his last few movies, The Dog Stars, Gladiator II, and Napoleon all failed to dazzle at the box office, but there was a time when seeing his name on a poster meant a movie was a guaranteed hit.

Sources indicate that back in 2015, Scott teamed up with Matt Damon for The Martian, which is an adaptation of the best-selling sci-fi book of the same name from author Andy Weir, who also wrote the book that inspired Ryan Gosling's Project Hail Mary. The Martian is currently without a streaming home in America right now, but the demand to watch the movie at home is higher than ever. So many fans are renting or purchasing The Martian on Apple TV that it has now been in the top 10 for over 100 days now.

Industry observers note that the Martian and Project Hail Mary are quite similar, which makes sense considering both books were written by the same author, but there are some important differences. Both tales center around an astronaut who is lost millions of miles from home, but while The Martian follows Mark Watney's journey to make it back to Earth with his life, Project Hail Mary follows Ryland Grace as he attempts to save humanity from a dangerous race of space algae known as Astrophage. Project Hail Mary also features an alien named Rocky, and the film is considered a much harder sci-fi than its 2015 predecessor.

Check out The Martian on VOD platforms like Prime Video and Apple TV, and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Matt Damon and Ridley Scott's future projects.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • iOS 27.3 releases next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.
  • Apple is granting iPhone Duo people one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.
  • Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient newly introduced option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27.3 releases next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo people one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient newly introduced option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:.

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to rapidly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

Recent findings suggest that if your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most consumers, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

Industry observers note that on a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds latest face unlock feature for iPhone Duo.

In a recent development, reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great newly introduced option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use.

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that consumers have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and latest keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:.

In a recent development, iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z.

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level.
  • “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump remarked.
  • Trump mentioned Georgia and Fresh Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump said his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump remarked. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

Trump mentioned Georgia and Fresh Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he mentioned, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Recent findings suggest that trump said his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

Sources indicate that the bill’s sponsors announced more than 60 new House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he mentioned, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she noted in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

Recent findings suggest that A floor vote has yet to be confirmed, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

Sources indicate that for crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s fresh Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.

Apple TV's 30-Episode Space Opera Masterpiece Is An S-Tier Sci-Fi Series

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that space may be infinite, but truly incredible space operas are anything but.
  • Recent findings suggest that loosely based on Isaac Asimov's book series of the same name, Apple TV's Foundation is not another run-of-the-mill, bottom-tier sci-fi show.
  • Foundation season 1 earned a mixed reception from viewers and critics, with many calling out its extreme creative liberties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that space may be infinite, but truly incredible space operas are anything but. For there are thousands of galaxies and parallel worlds in the sci-fi genre, but only a few are worth getting lost in. There lies the magic of one of Apple TV's greatest sci-fi shows. It immerses viewers in a space opera so grand and scintillating that it is almost impossible not to be in complete awe.

Recent findings suggest that loosely based on Isaac Asimov's book series of the same name, Apple TV's Foundation is not another run-of-the-mill, bottom-tier sci-fi show. Its sheer brilliance lies in its ability to significantly drift away from its source material. And, yet, somehow retain the essence of Asimov's scale and themes. Unlike most epic sci-fi demonstrates, Foundation initially stumbled and struggled to find its feet.

Foundation season 1 earned a mixed reception from viewers and critics, with many calling out its extreme creative liberties. However, just when it looked like the Apple TV series would turn into another forgotten sci-fi adaptation, it leveled up like a caterpillar discovering its wings. Although still a little divisive among book readers, Foundation is undoubtedly an S-tier sci-fi series.

Instead of delivering a direct page-to-page translation of Asimov's books, Apple TV's Foundation uses the original sprawling universe as, quite literally, its "foundation." Since "the beginning of wisdom is the definition of terms," Foundation arms itself with the Socratic method and borrows some of the core concepts from the source material, including psychohistory.

In a recent development, then, it ingeniously takes a detour and adds a lot of original lore to the mix. One of the biggest challenges with adapting Isaac Asimov's stories was that they span across centuries. The Apple TV series does not completely abandon the original long-term storytelling. However, it also refuses to change its main characters every few chapters like the books.

Industry observers note that the show seems to understand that, in audiovisual storytelling, viewers need long-term rootable characters. A narrative cannot merely survive on abstract ideas, mathematical predictions, history, and constantly shifting perspectives. Owing to this, Apple TV's Foundation introduced everything from cloning to digital consciousness to be able to have more long-running character arcs.

It must be noted, though, that the Apple TV sci-fi show is not the best adaptation. In 3 seasons, so far, it has drifted far enough from the books to be seen as its own thing. While there are still some overlaps between Asimov's novels and the TV series, the show is better off being treated as an original and S-tier addition to sci-fi in its own right.

Sources indicate that one of Foundation's biggest strengths is its epic visual flair. Like most sci-fi shows on Apple TV, Foundation does not look like it is bogged down by limited small-screen budgets. Even some of the most abstract ideas from the original books are captured with such brilliant tangibility in the series that it is hard not to forgive it for its creative liberties.

From the colossal Star Bridge collapsing onto Trantor to the brutalist geometry of "The Vault" on Terminus, every frame is stunning with immense attention to detail and realism.

When these visuals are paired with Bear McCreary’s compositions, Apple TV's Foundation almost feels as grand and mythic as movies like Dune and Interstellar. It can still be debated whether the sci-fi space opera should have taken such a significant leap with its creative liberties. After all, an "adaptation" is only as good as its ability to "adapt.".

But perhaps that is exactly where the real genius of the Apple TV sci-fi series lies. It does not merely change its source material to dumb down its story for the screen. Despite the changes, it is still an intelligent space opera that understands that fresh ideas and worlds are waiting to be born out of Isaac Asimov's brilliant literary works.

Isaac Asimov's novel series is brought to life in Foundation, a television adaptation of the epic sci-fi saga created for Apple TV+. The show follows a group of exiled humans that find themselves as the last chance to save the Galactic Empire, primarily from itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The uproar over the alleged use of generative AI imagery in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” has taken a familiar path. Early responses to the Netflix film penned by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher have pointed out egregious examples of generative video artifacts sticking out in key flashback moments in the film — including one shot from the trailer where it certainly looks like a video AI program rendered a wagon the wrong way around.

According to recent reports, the criticism is of the use of generative AI in principle as a fundamental betrayal of the creative process — but it’s also of Fincher, as a director who, historically, has been meticulous with the level of detail and intention in every single shot of his films. In the early responses to Fincher’s latest, there’s been a lot of surprise and disappointment about this particular filmmaker being caught up in an AI controversy. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

It has been revealed that at first blush, his approach seems at odds with using generative AI video, which relies on regurgitated (and, it bears repeating every time, stolen) data. But Fincher has defended his use of AI to the LA Times as a way to continue to innovate on an art form that is, after all, just over a hundred years old.

Industry observers note that that defense really shouldn’t be surprising, given Fincher’s history with AI specifically. Although he’s been critical of generative tools in the past, Fincher admitted to using them (never publicly disclosing which) in the 4K remaster of “Se7en,” which the director described as a process of needing to remake the negative in order to battle the ravages of time (and the thousands of tiny scratches that would show up in 4K). “If you could see a 30-year-old negative and what it looks like even when immaculately stored — it was an enormous amount of fixing, just digs and scratches and cinch,” he told EW at the time.

That kind of image restoration technology was around long, long before the Anthropic IPO failed to save the stock market, but its level of precision has increased enormously in the past year. There were also sequences in the stored “Se7en,” though, where generative tech filled in gaps from the original. For one example, Fincher talked about a moment where a camera pan overshot the mark and changedh a shot. The performance had been good enough to use a technically flawed take — and, combined wit an unused take, allowed software to generate the missing information and restore the intended image.

Sources indicate that “It ends up being the most thrillingly stupid fix in the world because if you see it, we didn’t do our jobs. And you probably won’t see it. You probably won’t be aware that it’s happened. But you look at it, and you just think to yourself, ‘It’s so nice that we can fix that kind of stuff today,'” Fincher told Collider about that moment in “Se7en.”.

In a recent development, by Fincher’s own lights, then, the problem with AI in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is that people are painfully aware of it. AI critics might make a distinction between video restoration tools that work on existing projects and those tools being used because they can more quickly and cheaply generate originals that would’ve otherwise needed to be crafted by human hands. Having something AI-generated isn’t necessarily better than nothing when it comes to art, and choosing to AI-generate a Western chase sequence inside of, say, 10 seconds isn’t a solution to all.

It has been revealed that still, Fincher knows what he’s doing. This past week, he emphasized to the LA Times that he’s not a Luddite when it comes to film: “We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old, and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?”.

The answer is an emphatic “No!” to some And they can certainly be mad, or disappointed, or disheartened about Fincher’s decision to use AI tools. The one thing they shouldn’t be is surprised.
