  • Her name is December, and one of the things she remembers is a plague that the people she loves have yet to live through.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews newly introduced releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Brandon Sanderson has given some thought to what he’d do if he woke up as a teenager with all his adult memories intact: he’d happily pass on the opportunity. “I’ve read too many stories about time travel and it never goes well,” the Mistborn author told Woman’s World. He did, however, get out of bed the next morning and write two chapters of a book about a woman who wakes up on her 21st birthday with an entire lifetime to reconsider.

Her name is December, and one of the things she remembers is a plague that the people she loves have yet to live through. She sets out on the River Violet to warn the king’s court, with a priestess and an aspiring fashion designer for company. Getting a royal official to take the word of a 21-year-old seriously is an immediate concern, but the harder one is deciding what to change. December can remember the people she lost, but she also knows whom she fell in love with and the children she had. Saving someone now could cost her the chance to meet somebody else later.

Tor Books will publish the U.S. hardcover of Brandon Sanderson’s The Fires of December on Tuesday, December 8. The 384-page edition brings the standalone Cosmere novel to bookstore shelves after an earlier release through Sanderson’s Hoid’s Storybook Collection crowdfunding campaign. Readers who prefer a physical copy can preorder the Tor edition now, while the ebook and audiobook have been available to the public since October 6, with longtime Mistborn narrator Michael Kramer reading the audio edition.

It has been revealed that four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

Sources indicate that you belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

It has been revealed that you want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

Recent findings suggest that you would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

In a recent development, you can start with December. Sanderson groups the book with Tress of the Emerald Sea and Yumi and the Nightmare Painter under the name Hoid’s Travails. The three share a narrator in Hoid, the storyteller who turns up across the Cosmere, but each follows a different lead and tells a complete story. Readers can pick them up in any order, including anyone still working through The Stormlight Archive who’d like to spend a weekend elsewhere in Sanderson’s universe.

It has been revealed that sanderson had already tried two other ideas for a secret project before December came to him. Once he had those opening chapters, he wrote the first draft in about a month and printed a copy for his wife, the first person he wanted to share it with. Those same chapters are now available on his website, along with the reading he gave at Dragonsteel Nexus. It’s a good place to hear Hoid tell this one from the beginning, back when December’s biggest question about the River Violet was whether there really was a demon upstream supplying all that blood.

The Fires of December releases December 8.

Up until 2017, The Legend of Zelda entries focused more on a semi-open and non-linear formula, but despite receiving some criticism for its artstyle, both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom were praised for their stunning maps that were full to the brim with activities, especially the latter which introduced brand-latest mechanics such as construction.

So much so, that our very own Cody Gravelle awarded it a perfect 10/10, with his review reading:.

Recent findings suggest that if it's time to move on from the Tears of the Kingdom Hyrule that's now spanned two games, it hasn't overstayed its welcome. The memories this game is capable of creating just because of its ambitious systems mean that no two players will ever have the same experience - except that of joy, and the excitement that comes with unknown possibilities. Anyone worried that there would be some fatal flaw that came to ruin what seemed to be a can't-miss Switch launch can now rest easy. Tears of the Kingdom is a monumental achievement, and it's going to be talked about relentlessly for years to come.

With reports previously suggesting that the Wilds' subseries had come to an end after just two entries, it seems as though this may not have been the truth, as recent leaks suggest that a third entry may right now be in development at Nintendo.

The news comes as a shock, considering that Nintendo is not known for making direct sequels, let alone a three-part series, but it seems as though the success of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom may just have made the decision for the company.

During episode 294 of the Xbox Era Podcast, Shpeshal Nick and Jeff Grubb discussed rumors over a potential third installment in the Wilds subseries, and according to them, it will include even more dimension hopping which will expand the open-world even further.

Of course, these rumors should be taken with a pinch of salt, as Nintendo has not hinted at potentially continuing the Wilds' subseries into the future. #108548. Dungeon Crawler Carl Breaks One Of Fantasy's Biggest Unwritten Rules

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (425 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Screenrant ↗ Open Full Page

Dungeon Crawler Carl Breaks One Of Fantasy's Biggest Unwritten Rules

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (425 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dungeon Crawler Carl is arguably one of the most successful modern science fantasy IPs in recent memory, with author Matt Dinniman's universe growing to eight massive novels since its humble beginnings as a self-published project on Royal Road.
  • According to recent reports, dungeon Crawler Carl's world-building, character backstories, and unexpected array of enemies, allies, and aliens are just the beginning of what makes the story so special.
  • These aren't just simple polls about favorite characters or potential storylines, and Dinniman gives readers different possibilities for everything from enemies and rewards to locations, names, and other unexpected details.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dungeon Crawler Carl is arguably one of the most successful modern science fantasy IPs in recent memory, with author Matt Dinniman's universe growing to eight massive novels since its humble beginnings as a self-published project on Royal Road. Dinniman has always had a relatively unique and unconventional approach to storytelling, but one that has captivated readers more and more with each upcoming installment.

According to recent reports, dungeon Crawler Carl's world-building, character backstories, and unexpected array of enemies, allies, and aliens are just the beginning of what makes the story so special. One of the most interesting aspects of how the story has evolved over its lifetime is that many of the most unique and outlandish details aren't even created by Dinniman alone. The author actually breaks a longstanding "unwritten rule" among fantasy/sci-fi writers, and it's safe to say that the creative choice has paid off time and time again.

These aren't just simple polls about favorite characters or potential storylines, and Dinniman gives readers different possibilities for everything from enemies and rewards to locations, names, and other unexpected details. Some of these decisions are relatively minor, while others have ended up playing notable roles in the larger narrative. In many cases, the results have even caught Dinniman himself off guard.

Importantly, this doesn't mean readers are deciding what Carl does or what Donut says. Dinniman maintains creative control over his characters and their decisions, instead allowing fans to influence the external circumstances they encounter. He then has to figure out how to incorporate those choices into the story, even when readers select something completely unexpected.

It's a fairly unconventional approach to writing a fantasy series, and one that breaks the "unwritten rule" that many fantasy authors follow of keeping the world-building elements of the story very intentional and deliberate. In many ways, Dinniman allows readers to throw him curveballs as some sort of a challenge to himself to make these things work on the page, and so far there are countless examples of how it's paid off.

Some of the most notable examples include:.

Beyond Patreon, Dinniman has also incorporated suggestions from fellow writers. Author Steve Rowland, the troll stripper in the Desperado Club, was named after real-life fantasy author S.L. Rowland, who jokingly suggested his own name when Dinniman requested stripper names on Twitter.

It's pretty incredible how many beloved elements of Dungeon Crawler Carl would have been completely different without fans contributing to the creative process, and it's a major piece of what makes the series so special.

#108543. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1289 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you know “the look” by now.
  • At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • It has been revealed that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

It has been revealed that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

In a recent development, the problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Industry observers note that those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

Industry observers note that this pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

According to recent reports, if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

Recent findings suggest that to a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

Sources indicate that that means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

#108541. Netflix's 4-Hour Fantasy Series Is The Closest Thing To A Live-Action D&D Show

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (643 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Screenrant ↗ Open Full Page

Netflix's 4-Hour Fantasy Series Is The Closest Thing To A Live-Action D&D Show

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Considering it's such a massive part of pop culture, Dungeons & Dragons hasn't found much success in the live-action realm.
  • According to recent reports, on the small screen, it's a washout.
  • Four years ago, however, Netflix did release a short-lived fantasy series that, from a certain angle, is a live-action Dungeons & Dragons adaptation in all but name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Considering it's such a massive part of pop culture, Dungeons & Dragons hasn't found much success in the live-action realm. The 2000s movies are notorious, although perhaps earn a place in the 'so bad they're good' category, and while the more recent Honor Among Thieves brought joy to all, smiles in theaters didn't quite translate into great chests full of box office gold.

According to recent reports, on the small screen, it's a washout. Animated shows inspired by Dungeons & Dragons have enjoyed great success, especially the Critical Role universe on Prime Video, but as far as live-action is concerned, Stranger Things is as good as it gets. Netflix has announced a proper live-action Dungeons & Dragons project on the horizon in the shape of Ravenloft, which is currently being developed and makes history as the first true Dungeons & Dragons TV series in live-action.

Four years ago, however, Netflix did release a short-lived fantasy series that, from a certain angle, is a live-action Dungeons & Dragons adaptation in all but name.

According to recent reports, netflix's primary The Witcher series (the one where Henry Cavill gets possessed by the soul of a Hemsworth brother halfway through) shares very little in common with Dungeons & Dragons. The show, unsurprisingly, feels more like a video game than a tabletop campaign, placing a single protagonist in the spotlight and focusing heavily on visual spectacle alongside a political landscape somewhere between Middle-earth and Westeros.

2022's The Witcher: Blood Origin recalibrates the same fictional world through a Dungeons & Dragons lens. You get the ragtag group of adventurers, all with different cultural backgrounds, skills, and weapons. Compared to its parent series, Blood Origin's streamlined story also flows more like a campaign, as the party works to thwart one central enemy locked in his fortress. Decisions are made that will affect future campaigns to come (i.e. the creation of the first Witcher), and there's an uptick in humor that draws more inspiration from the world of Dungeons & Dragons than The Witcher itself. There's even a charismatic Dungeon Master of sorts, as Jaskier acts as the story's narrator.

The problem with The Witcher: Blood Origin, of course, is that not many people like it. In fairness, the spinoff has its highlights. Meldof the Dwarf proves an inspired addition, and the four-part story certainly can't be accused of lacking ambition. At the same time, Blood Origin buckles under the weight of propping up The Witcher's future, and Jaskier's inclusion feels jarringly unnecessary.

Sources indicate that the burden of setting up new storylines for the main series, combined with the relatively short season, results in a tale with more exposition than character depth, and Lenny Henry's villain suffers most of all. Blood Origin wants viewers to care about how the prequel will impact Geralt and co. in the future, but that comes at the expense of letting the audience care about the spinoff characters themselves in the present.

Without the kind of substance that would justify a spinoff happening in the first place, even The Witcher: Blood Origin's historic events fall flat. The creation of the very first Witcher and the Conjunction of the Spheres pass by like relatively mundane events. The viewer needs to almost jolt themselves into remembering these are foundational events of The Witcher's universe playing out before their eyes, and not just seven unlucky heroes having a bad day.

Needless to say, the world will expect a little more from Ravenloft, especially with it being TV's first proper live-action Dungeons & Dragons venture. The failure of The Witcher: Blood Origin gives a clear lesson that the new series cannot rely solely on its famous universe and franchise connections, and should instead concoct a story and group of characters that would feel just as compelling if they existed outside Dungeons & Dragons altogether.

Industry observers note that you know we're cooking when the soundbar has "ultra" in its name. Like Ultraman, but less villainous. This glass-topped beauty features Dolby Atmos built in for some extra dimension to your favorite movies — and its $350 off. That's meg... I mean Ultra. It's Ultra.

This one's also got Ultra in the name, so you know it must be good. It is — and we love the upcoming design. The Bose Lifestyle Ultra Soundbar looks like a spaceship. If spaceships were small enough to fit on a TV stand. You never know; the aliens might be tiny. Either way, $200 off a brand new soundbar with excellent Dolby Atmos and great style is nothing to sniff at.

In a recent development, tammy's reviews and buying guide expertise have more focus than ever on Tom's Guide, helping buyers find the audio gear that works best for them. Tammy has worked with some of the most desirable audio brands on the planet in her time writing about headphones, speakers, and more, bringing a consumer focussed approach to critique and buying advice. Away from her desk, you'll probably find her in the countryside writing (extremely bad) poetry, or putting her screenwriting Masters to good use creating screenplays that'll never see the light of day.

#108535. Recasting 10 ‘The Office’ Characters for 2026

Recasting 10 ‘The Office’ Characters for 2026

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in 2005, NBC debuted the American version of The Office, the hit British mockumentary created by Ricky Gervais and Stephen Merchant.
  • Recent findings suggest that while The Paper has continued the cinematic universe, one might wonder what would happen if, in an alternate universe, The Office debuted in 2026.
  • Recent findings suggest that for seven seasons, The Office's fearless leader was the one and only Michael Scott.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in 2005, NBC debuted the American version of The Office, the hit British mockumentary created by Ricky Gervais and Stephen Merchant. With the first season a near carbon copy of its transatlantic counterpart, the first six episodes were a smash, leading to a long, prosperous run where it formed its own identity. For nine incredible seasons, the series made us laugh, cringe, and laugh some more. Though it was disappointing when it ended, it became one of the most-streamed series after its run.

Recent findings suggest that while The Paper has continued the cinematic universe, one might wonder what would happen if, in an alternate universe, The Office debuted in 2026. To many, it remains a largely untouchable show with a pitch-perfect ensemble, but we're here to dream! We'll take 10 roles and explore the perfect cast if it had been made today. Based on the characters' traits, this fantasy casting is just that. While no one can truly replicate the originals' brilliance, these individuals would honor the characters while bringing their own signature flair. Who would you like to see round out the ensemble beyond these 10?

Recent findings suggest that for seven seasons, The Office's fearless leader was the one and only Michael Scott. Serving as the regional manager of the Scranton branch of Dunder Mifflin, Michael's management style is often incompetent, inappropriate, and disruptive. And yet, he is an extraordinary salesman. Beneath his self-aggrandizing, egotistical, and socially tone-deaf persona lies deep insecurity, loneliness, and a desperate desire to be loved. He often tries to act hip and cool, but it's usually met with rolled eyes and awkward silence. Played to perfection by the incomparable Steve Carell, Michael remains one of the greatest characters ever created in television history. Carell was far from his British counterpart, David Brent (Ricky Gervais), instead becoming a melancholic comedy hero whom the audience could actually root for. His growth arc meant that when he left, it was a victory for the character.

Carell played Michael straight with full commitment. He genuinely made Michael believe he was a hilarious, smooth, beloved "cool boss," completely blinded to reality. While no one could replicate the same energy he brought, a good option in the same vein would be the brilliant Sam Richardson. As seen as Richard Splett in Veep and Aniq in The Afterparty, Richardson is a master of weaponized naivety. He is the undisputed king of playing characters who are fiercely well-meaning but completely out of their depth. His ability to deliver cringe-worthy, tone-deaf lines with bright, innocent optimism makes him impossible to hate. In a 2026 iteration, the office environment would look drastically different, so his Michael would be a modern LinkedIn Influencer Manager who would try to implement modern workplace trends, probably a leading force for AI, only to drastically misunderstand and use it inappropriately. Like Carell, Richardson has elite improvisational skills as a Second City alum. He could capture the fast-talking spiral with perfect comedic rhythm, bringing an expressive face built for mockumentary-style satire. Richardson possesses an undeniable warmth and would bring genuine moments of vulnerability. You'd root for Richardson's Michael in the same way you fell in love with Carell's.

According to recent reports, call him Assistant Regional Manager or Assistant to the Regional Manager, but whatever you call him, just know he's a hilarious menace. Dwight Schrute is an intensely competitive, socially awkward, overly loyal-to-authority, top-selling paper salesman who delivers unique eccentricities daily. At Dunder Mifflin, he pulls endless office pranks and maintains a long-standing rivalry with Jim Halpert (John Krasinski). Outside the office, he owns and operates a beet farm alongside his delightfully unique cousin Mose (Mike Schur). He's also a survivalist, martial arts enthusiast, and weapons lobbyist. Brought to life by Rainn Wilson, he committed completely to Dwight's absolute deadpan sincerity, theatrical intensity, and rigid lack of self-awareness. Even his notorious physical appearance and intense gaze became a major part of his identity.

In a recent development, dwight is a character that needs to balance cruelty with humanity. He had an odd kindness to him. Having an individual who can tap into that while also embracing robotic physicality and mastery of improv is crucial. The perfect pick would be comedian Chris Fleming. Having Fleming play Dwight would be a stroke of modern comedic genius. The landscape of "weird" has evolved, and Fleming would bring a surreal terror to the 2026 iteration. Fleming activates a specialized manic, aggressive, and highly localized intensity, much like his character Gayle Waters-Waters in the YouTube series Gayle. If you've seen his HBO stand-up special, Chris Fleming: Live at the Palace, you'll see why his brand of humor fits perfectly into Dwight's unique world. He'll give you a full-bodied, rubbery performance. There, he even showcased his version of the reaction face when he stared down the barrel of the camera. As a performer who relies on hyper-specific, multi-layered observational humor, he can build an entire worldview from something seemingly mundane. Fleming has the zeal needed to make Dwight come back to life.

With all the chaos happening inside the office, someone had to hold down the fort for the normal ones! That man was Jim Halpert. A witty, easygoing sales rep, Jim was known for his deadpan humor, harmless pranks on seatmate Dwight, and breaking the fourth wall at every opportunity. Oh, and his beautiful romance with Pam Beesly (Jenna Fischer). John Krasinski brought a perfectly grounded Everyman charm that made him absolutely beloved. With natural comedic timing and an ability to be completely wholesome with a flash of a smile, Krasinski transformed Jim into the epitome of a sitcom leading man. Striking the right balance of humor and heart, Krasinski transitioned Jim from bored prankster to sincere husband and father, maturing into a working adult by series end.

Industry observers note that should The Office be cast in 2026, we would begin with Jim's arc from the start of the series. Thus, our Jim must have the precise mix of boyish charm, natural sarcasm, and expressive physicality. To play Dunder Mifflin's favorite prankster, it's Jacob Bertrand. Best known for his high-energy role as Hawk in Cobra Kai, Bertrand has the right toolkit to play the relatable, slightly unmotivated entry-level salesman navigating early adulthood. With an expressive face, Bertrand can bring that Jim smirk to the camera, and you'll instantly fall for his charm. He can bring high-intensity when needed, but his subtlety is a great strength. Naturally, he's a laid-back individual who could capture the smartest guy in the room without exposing it or trying too hard. Bertrand's inherent personality has a likability and puppy-dog nature that would make people root for him. With a lanky frame and strong physical awareness, Bertrand would easily transform into Jim in a heartbeat.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

It has been revealed that you belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

It has been revealed that you belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

Recent findings suggest that you belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

It has been revealed that the Office reflected the reality of what life inside a boring, cubicle-filled environment was like. But when you walked into Dunder Mifflin, your day was brightened when you saw Pam Beesly sitting at reception. Pam starts the series as a quiet, long-suffering receptionist before becoming a strong salesperson. Much of her allure was watching the slow-burn romance and eventual marriage to Jim Halpert. That is, once she left her first fiancé, Roy Anderson (David Denman). That allowed her to grow from a timid, unconfident young woman into a self-assured, artistic, and assertive individual. Jenna Fischer drew on her own real-life experience as a struggling actress to bring unmatched authenticity, quiet patience, and lived-in relatability. Her power came through subtle acting and expressive silence. She understood that Pam was stuck in a subordinate position where her only means of expressing herself was through micro-expressions and side-eye.

In a recent development, fischer ensured that Pam was beloved by all. She gave her a down-to-earth, everyday quality with remarkable chemistry. To take on the other half of the iconic couple, look no further than Madison Iseman. As a modern girl next door, Iseman balances relatable charm with subtle comedic timing that suits Pam. Iseman has built a career playing accessible, sympathetic characters like Bethany Walker in the reboot Jumanji film series. Now starring in The Rainmaker, the same whip-smart intellect she gives to Sarah would translate perfectly for Pam. Pam needs Iseman's dry wit when she sits idly by as Jim pranks Dwight. She'll be a passive observer or an eager contributor when the situation calls for it. Iseman has a flourishing career, but she's still got a fresh face to balance out the part.

It has been revealed that being a temp is not fun, but most of us know it is what it is: temporary. Then there was Ryan Howard, who seemingly made a career out of sticking around way longer than a temp should. He starts his time at Dunder Mifflin as a young, soft-spoken temp, acting as the grounded audience surrogate. Over time, the office got to him, and he evolved into an arrogant, hip, and deeply pretentious corporate climber. Perhaps Michael's obsession with making him his protégé was to blame. He is defined by his toxic, on-again, off-again romance with Kelly Kapoor (Mindy Kaling) and his glorious fall from grace in the corporate world. Ryan was one of those characters you loved to watch because you never knew where B.J. Novak was about to take him. He was a fish out of water at first, but the truth is, his DNA was meant for Dunder Mifflin. Novak blended dry, deadpan sarcasm with a masterclass in inflated ego and failing upward.

As a key writer on the show, Novak built Ryan to suit him. Now, using the blueprint that Novak built, the right actor to follow in his footsteps is Griffin Gluck. Mastering the too-cool-for-this deadpan energy, Gluck brings the right youthful charm, comedic timing, and low-key chaotic energy needed to pull off Ryan's descent from relatable temp to a pretentious 2026 tech-bro version of the character. As seen in projects like American Vandal and Big Time Adolescence, Gluck knows how to bring understated reactions. He can easily portray someone who thinks they're entirely above working at a mid-tier paper tech giant while quietly absorbing all the dysfunction around him for sport. Gluck has a smooth-talking prowess that makes you believe he's the shit, but truly, it's a facade. Having played parts navigating messy, awkward relationships, Gluck could tap into that young adult relationship that is the antithesis of Pam and Jim. Gluck can capture the deeply uncomfortable feeling of being a yes-man to Michael, who is trying to be "woke" yet never telling him how wrong he is. Gluck is a rising star and the epitome of Ryan Howard.

Recent findings suggest that every office has a relentless flirt, and at Dunder Mifflin, that title went to Kelly Kapoor. As the branch's customer service rep, Kelly could talk your ear off. And yes, she did. She is known for being dramatic, obsessed with pop culture, celebrity gossip, fashion, and Ryan Howard. Her high-drama romantic relationships were a massive part of her identity. Whether it was her on-again, off-again relationship with Ryan or her infamous fling with Darryl Philbin (Craig Robinson), Kelly's love life was a hot-button topic because everyone knew about it. Kelly was played by Mindy Kaling, one of the show's writers, which allowed her the freedom to play and develop her infamous voice and wildly narcissistic yet lovable traits. Kelly was built out of pure satire, insecurity, charm, and a total lack of self-awareness, making her a hilarious contrast to the more grounded, dreary "adults" in the room.

Industry observers note that kelly is the life of The Office. To capture that spirit, you need an actress of the same caliber. Look no further than Maitreyi Ramakrishnan. She's simply perfect because she's literally embodied Kelly on social media. Oh, and she also took part in Kaling's Netflix comedy Never Have I Ever. So, she's essentially "Mini Mindy!" Ramakrishnan can make Kelly the blueprint for modern unhinged confidence and internet-era attention-seeking. With all the social media she would be attached to, she'll be on her phone more than doing her actual job. Ramakrishnan excels at playing a sharp, fast-talking, unapologetically dramatic young woman who lives in their own fantasy. After starring in Best of the Best, Ramakrishnan has moved into more mature parts while honoring her heritage. Kaling broke ground as a South Asian actress on sitcoms, so continuing the cultural lineage is crucial. Ramakrishnan would represent a fresh, punchy comedic voice of the new generation.

The new era of The Office officially kicked off with the arrival of Andy Bernard, the Regional Director of Sales at Dunder Mifflin's Stamford branch prior to the merger. Andy is known for being a "Nard Dog," an obsessive fan of a cappella music, and a hot-headed, insecure, and status-obsessed employee. While it took him some time to mesh with the crew, Andy eventually became an essential member of the team. Ed Helms combined cringe-worthy overconfidence with a deep, unvarnished emotional vulnerability that made Andy an oddly magnetic character. He was an amalgam of annoyance, turning everyday pretension into high comedy. You cheered for him as you simultaneously shook your head at his antics. After his anger management reset, the new iteration of Andy was a sweet, well-meaning doofus trying to fit in, bridging the emotional gap following Carell's departure.

Industry observers note that helms played Andy as a glorious, vulnerable fool who wore his heart on his sleeve. To take on Andy, a music-loving charmer would be the perfect fit for the part. Andy needs to have inherent theatricality, and Jordan Fisher has just that. Fisher, known for his role in Teen Beach Movie, winning Dancing with the Stars, and his time on Broadway in shows like Hamilton, Dear Evan Hansen, Hadestown, and the upcoming Purple Rain, can channel the over-the-top, performance-ready energy into a corporate setting. He would embody the exhausting, hilarious reality of someone who treats a mid-tier paper company like the grandest stage. Andy is known for his random yet flawless riffs and pitch-perfect a capella, which Fisher would master. Fisher would ease into the peppy Ivy League grad who is stuck in the past, yet exudes corny charisma. And when he needs to get dramatic, Fisher has the acting chops to tap into that. Fisher's versatility would bring Andy to 2026.

Sources indicate that what made The Office tick was its ability to give once-background players main character energy. One standout was Angela Martin, the senior head accountant and infamous head of the Party Planning Committee — a position she took far too seriously. Angela is a fun killer. She is cold, stern, hyper-judgmental, rigid, and intensely conservative. She doesn't like anyone's antics, especially if they are meant to be her partner. And don't forget her obsession with her cats. Just don't call her a cat lady! She has an affinity for condescending to her coworkers. Although she can dish it, she certainly can't take it. From a secretive affair with Dwight to a brief engagement to Andy and a short-lived marriage to the Senator, Robert Lipton (Jack Coleman), love was never quite on her side. What made Angela great was Angela Kinsey. Though there is a sharp contrast between her real-life personality and her character's icy demeanor, Kinsey's ability to bring a hilarious feistiness is why we loved to hate her. She truly was that co-worker that every office despises.

It has been revealed that with sharp, deadpan, judgmental reactions, Angela was a key cog in the comedy. While the role was centered around the actress, tapping another performer who can bring that same Angela DNA to the forefront would be perfect. That actress is Aimee Teegarden. Widely remembered for her good girl persona as Julie Taylor in Friday Night Lights, an older Teegarden would be able to subvert the sweet, wholesome, small-town girl next door facade for a tightly wound vibe. Teegarden's skill set could capture the passive-aggressive hypocrisy in a masterful, multi-layered comedic performance. Teegarden's extensive recent work in poised Hallmark romance roles would translate to a character obsessed with order, rules, and finding the right guy. Visually, Teegarden can take her petite, classic blonde aesthetic and effortlessly pull off the cardigans, tightly pinned hair, and judgmental side-eye. Teegarden is the upcoming era Angela.

When Pam got her promotion, it seemed impossible to replace the irreplaceable receptionist. Then Erin Hannon showed up, and an equally delightful young woman brought a new energy to the desk. Erin is a cheerful, naive, and fiercely optimistic receptionist whose real name is Kelly. But when she was hired, new boss Charles Miner (Idris Elba) noticed the confusion with Kelly Kapoor, so she agreed to go by her middle name. Erin brought a quirky, childlike quality that allowed her deep-seated enthusiasm to take over. Delightfully perky, Ellie Kemper injected pure joy into Erin, helping reenergize the series. What was meant as a temporary arc transformed into a beloved fixture in the office. Kemper's innocent sincerity became a staple of her character.

Industry observers note that her refreshing color and harmless naïveté were a welcome addition to the painfully awkward and mundane environment. To play Erin in 2026, the perfect casting would be the delightfully perky Jade Pettyjohn. An absolute masterstroke of alignment, Pettyjohn brings an exuberant, bubbly optimism to the screen, countered by a deep, underlying vulnerability. Pettyjohn sits perfectly in that generational sweet spot, capturing the right workplace dynamic as a bridge between younger and older co-workers. She has flawless comedic roots, having anchored Nickelodeon's School of Rock as Summer Hathaway. She knows how to play into the snappy, high-energy sitcom delivery and deadpan reaction shots. Raised in the foster system, Erin has a childlike innocence and eagerness to please, which Pettyjohn delivered during her run as Lexie Richardson in Little Fires Everywhere. She can capture the sheltered suburban overachiever with a heart of gold. Even in more dramatic shows like Significant Sky, Monsters: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story, and Grey's Anatomy, Pettyjohn has the chops to make Erin's emotional breakthrough feel grounded.

In a recent development, shout out to everyone who works in human resources because it must be one of the most universally despised positions in any office. At least that's how it was portrayed on The Office! At Dunder Mifflin's Scranton branch, the head of HR was held by Toby Flenderson. A well-meaning man, Toby is soft-spoken, mild-mannered, and often a wet blanket who tries his hardest to enforce corporate policies, safety regulations, and workplace harmony. But with this lot, it was a near-impossible feat. Toby's defining dynamic was the intense, one-sided hatred from Michael Scott. He views him as a joyless, fun-sucking corporate enemy. Toby's joy in life is work because his personal life is anything but fun. Even when he's forced to Costa Rica, the island life is ruined when he breaks his neck zip-lining. Only Toby! What was essentially an accidental minor background player, Paul Lieberstein's brilliant performance evolved into a crucial piece of the puzzle. His ability to bring a genuine awkwardness and buzzkill energy to the screen was his greatest asset. As a writer on the series, Lieberstein knew the rhythm of the show, infusing Toby into the fold to suck the fun out when needed.

Lieberstein's natural camera-shyness and tendency to blush made him a perfect addition to the narrative. Toby was hated because Lieberstein played him so well. If you're looking for someone who plays someone you love to loathe, why not task someone who just so happened to play that type before, only younger? Look no further than Zach Woods, best known for playing Gabe Lewis on The Office! Let's face it, when Gabe grew up, he was destined to be Toby. Gabe was known for his extreme social awkwardness, sycophantic devotion to corporate authority figures like Jo Bennett (Kathy Bates), over-formal demeanor, and bizarre personal interests. Woods has made a name for himself for his sad boy energy. Like Jared Dunn in Silicon Valley, Woods captured the specific brand of quiet desperation and fragile compliance. Woods would bring a fresh take on the corporate punching bag. Woods is an expert at delivering rigid, overly corporate dialogue that no one is really tuned into. He would elevate the anxious, modern HR rep who tries desperately to do his job while no one cares to obey. Toby is the type of character who shrinks himself to avoid conflict. At 6'4", watching Woods try to physically do the same would be comedic gold. Now, part of the internet's obsession with Toby is the long-running fan theory that Toby is the "Scranton Strangler." Woods would certainly keep that theory alive! While some fans may be opposed to bringing back any of the original cast into newly introduced parts, Woods as Toby would be the most logical and seamless direction.

  • According to recent reports, would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

According to recent reports, would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

In a recent development, here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart swiftly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

Sources indicate that as if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber demonstrates up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Industry observers note that nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps.
  • Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable owners to generate nonconsensual nude images.
  • According to the updated rules, apps that allow users to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable owners to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow users to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”.

A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of Fresh Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta stated they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, remarked that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

According to recent reports, update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:.

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for owners. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”.

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The tech giant added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the firm said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

In a recent development, as for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The manufacturer said that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

In a recent development, enhancement, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:.

Apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps important complications and leaves out key context. The firm says it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

Sources indicate that there are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The company defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also says it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

Sources indicate that as for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out latest child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.
