📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

T here’s not a room in the world that could fit all of the trinkets, gifts, and prized possessions comedian Leslie Jones has accumulated through her career.

“I always keep something,” Jones says on Zoom from her Los Angeles home, panning the camera to show a wall of white shelves packed to the brim with tchotchkes. But it’s hard for her to pick favorites — especially since they all have treasured memories that go along with them. “Colin [Jost] gave me a trophy that remarked ‘Baddest Bitch in the World,’” she says with a laugh, pointing at the memento. “I’ve still got that one.”.

It has been revealed that jones might be one of the best-known late-bloomers in show business. In 2014, she joined Saturday Night Live as a writer before being promoted to a featured player. She was 47 at the time, making her the oldest person ever to join the cast. But even with two decades of stand-up work under her belt, slogging through bombed sets, late-night performances, and side hustles, Jones states she doesn’t regret her winding path to comedy fame. In fact, she’s adamant that if success had happened for her any sooner, she wouldn’t be here to talking to us. “I would have been a cautionary tale,” she says, plainly. “I would have made all the wrong decisions.”.

Sources indicate that jones spent five seasons on SNL, where she established herself as a comedic voice known for taking wild — and often foul-mouthed — swings at everything from dating during slavery to abortion bans to aims for her own funeral. This brash self-assuredness followed her even after her tenure, as she expanded her résumé to include TV and film roles in projects like Ghostbusters and Coming 2 America as well as professional fan duties — Chief Super Fan Commentator, to be precise — for NBC’s Olympics broadcasts. From her Upcoming York Times-bestselling memoir Leslie Fcking Jones to her latest gig hosting HGTV’s Roast My Rental (which debuted over the summer and re-airs through the end of November, and can be streamed on HBO Max), Jones has cemented herself as an outspoken and hilarious presence in pretty much any medium. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

“I’m making it work,” she says. “There’s no such thing as not waking up and getting some shit done.”.

For Rolling Stone’s Last Word column, Jones talked through nearly blowing off her SNL audition, vacation horror stories, and how to end the political divide in America.

What was your first job as a teenager?Damn, that took me way back. I worked at this place called Lounge Car Tours. My mom worked in accounting or something and she got me a job cleaning the buses. She tried to teach me how to drive her car, which was a stick, and I ran into one of the buses.

When did you realize comedy was for you? The first time I touched the mic. In college [at Colorado State University], I did the “funniest person on campus” contest. Whoever won got to open up for the comedians that were coming into town. When I was at that contest, I [felt] like, “Oh, I’ve already been doing this 10 years.”.

What’s the worst experience you’ve had bombing at a show?It was six months into me performing. This dude in the audience started heckling. I bombed and then I went back the next week. He was there, he didn’t say a word, and I still bombed.

How do you handle hecklers now? I tear they ass up. It depends on what type of heckler it is. If it’s a nice heckler, I’ll do something fun. But if it’s a mean or rude heckler, I try to make them feel like they’ll never speak again in public.

Sources indicate that what’s something you wish you had known early in your career?I don’t think I would have wanted to know, because I like that I learned my way. Maybe not to just make friends so easily. Don’t trust so easily. Related Content ‘SNL’: Watch Phoebe Bridgers Perform ‘Bobby,’ ‘Still Standing’ ‘SNL’: Hippie John Mulaney Has Some Very Unhip Thoughts at Woodstock ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Roasts Trump Admin Over Grounded Flights, Jensen Huang Affairs ‘SNL’ Cold Open: Jensen Huang, Tech CEOs Get a Crash Course in Female Spies.

According to recent reports, what was the first massive purchase that you made with your comedy money?Don’t laugh. I bought this Michael Kors purse. It was $300. I thought I was the shit. Then my friend was like, “Bitch, that’s just a Michael Kors purse. That’s not no Louis [Vuitton]. The fuck is wrong with you?”.

How does it feel in your body when you get a laugh from an audience?Like a high. Adrenaline. It’s a great feeling — ticklish.

Recent findings suggest that what’s the best advice you’ve ever gotten? November of ’87, I performed at this place called the World Comedy Club [in Times Square]. This comedian named Speedy had a show. Speedy’s best friends with Jamie Foxx, so Jamie came to close the show for him. I did that show. Did terrible. Bombed. I remember watching Jamie perform, going, “I got to figure out how he does this.” I had him in the corner like, “How do I become a better comic?” He was like, “How old are you?” I was 19. He was like, “You’re a baby. You don’t know anything. You don’t have no jokes. Go and live your life. Get your heart broken. Break hearts. Get fired. Get hired. Go live a life so you can have something to talk about.”.

According to recent reports, did you take the advice? Yeah. I was working. I was never trying to get a job to try to find myself — I was always trying to get a job to make money. I think young people have that equation wrong. I worked at Denny’s and then I sold perfume in the parking lot. I worked at the justice of the peace for a little, then the post office. Then I waitressed at Spoons [Grill & Bar, in Orange County]. I think I waited on [SNL cast member] Mikey Day while I was there. He used to go there all the time! I feel like I waited on him because [once I got to SNL], he had an obsession with me with his sketches. He would write sketches every time where I was either yelling at him or beating him up. I was like, “Mikey, do you want me to beat you up? Is this a thing you have?”.

Industry observers note that what’s your strongest memory from your SNL audition? Chris Rock got me the audition. He came in [to the Comedy Store in L.A.] one night, saw me perform, and then called me like two days later and was like, “Hey, I just had dinner with Lorne Michaels and he’s gonna call you for an audition for SNL.” I know he expected me to go crazy, but my brother had just died and I didn’t care about shit. When he called me, I went off on him. He said, “You’re a dumbass. Go to the fucking audition and do some jokes” and hung up. I called my manager livid — ”Fucking Chris Rock got me a fucking audition for SNL. How dare he?” My manager was like, “OK, I’m gonna need you to take a second to shut the fuck up. Have you lost your mind? Leslie, if you don’t go to that audition, I will quit.” I go to the Comedy Store just knowing I’m gonna find somebody that’s going to agree with me. And every comedian up there was looking at me like [I was] the dumbest motherfucker.

According to recent reports, we know how it ended — you were on the show for five seasons — but how did you spin that attitude in the room with Lorne?I was like, “You know what? I’m a go, so I can show them that I don’t need this shit.” Oh, God, the arrogance! By the end of that week, I wanted that job. I was so wrong. “There’s so much shit I can learn here.”.

I remember being in Indianapolis on the phone with my manager, and my manager was like, “Yeah, I think they’re gonna go with someone else, homie.” And I was like, “Yeah, I think so, too.” I was depressed. I was like, “Fuck. Do I take this job that my aunt is offering me? Because if I keep doing this, I ain’t gonna have no retirement money. I ain’t gonna be able to take care of myself when I get older. I’m 47 already, so maybe I should just go on back to Memphis and she can get me a job.” Then they called me.

In a recent development, how did you decide it was time to leave SNL?People try to act like they don’t know when they’re supposed to leave a situation. You know when you’re supposed to leave your job. You know when it’s time to move to the next level. If I was there when I was in my twenties, I would have stayed a long, long time just because I needed to learn and make money and get the connections. But [Lorne] got me when I was 47. And after five years of being there, I wasn’t ready to settle for that being my job the rest of my life. So it was, “If I don’t leave right now, I won’t be able to leave.”.

In a recent development, during the 2024 Paris Olympics, you were NBC’s Chief Super Fan Commentator. Are there any Olympic sports you feel you could make a solid attempt at?Oh, hell, no! Nah. The Olympics is the best of the best. There’s nothing I could do — maybe [jumping] around with the little ribbon.

On HGTV’s Roast My Rental, you help people fix up short-term homes. Do you have any of your own vacation-home or rental horror stories?Oh, yeah! I stayed in a place where they had a beehive in the wall. Then he had the nerve to say “Those bees wasn’t there before you got there.” Oh, so I brought the hive and climbed down a mountain, scaled up on the wall, and stuck that beehive right behind the bed? Yeah, that’s what I did.

Who are some people who’ve encouraged or supported you through your career? When I met them, they gave me great advice: Whoopi Goldberg, Arsenio Hall, Damon Wayans. Bill Bellamy, Greg Fitzsimmons. So many comedians.

How do you approach romantic relationships?What is that? A candy bar? That’s why I’m single now. I don’t approach them. I burn them down. I don’t know. You tell me.

Is there an album that corresponds to meaningful or transformative times in your life?Stevie Wonder, Talking Book. It has “Visions,” one of the best songs ever written. It’s the most beautiful, beautiful song. Stevie Wonder and Donny Hathaway are very important to me. I love music. My dad loved music. For a long time, he thought I was gonna be a musician because I knew music so well, just like he knew it. That’s back in the day when people used to write songs, write poetry. Now it’s just about how fast they can get into somebody’s drawers.

Recent findings suggest that are there any projects you’ve turned down that you wish you’d noted yes to?No. There’s projects that I said yes to that I wish I said no to.

Sources indicate that what are some of those?I ain’t gonna mention them. My publicist will be like, “God dammit, Leslie!”.

What’s a performance you’re proudest of? All my [Weekend] Updates on SNL. And there’s a sketch I did about the Upper East Side. I really am glad I did that — that’s one of my things I love the most.

What are some rules that you live by?Don’t shit where I eat — meaning don’t fuck people you work with. It’s the Number One rule because you will fuck your shit up. Don’t lend money. Just give it, because waiting on people to pay you back, you’re just gonna be frustrated. Passion at all times. Do everything with passion. Even if you’re folding your clothes. I can tell a person’s character just by how they fold their clothes. Always be intentional and enjoy everything — don’t skip days. Don’t say, “Hey, I can’t wait until it’s Tuesday.” Enjoy the days up until Tuesday.

Do you think you could have handled fame if it had happened to you when you started comedy at 19? No, absolutely not. Oh, thank you, Jesus. Thank you, Lord, for not letting me make it at 19. When you get stuff young, you stop creating. You stop growing. It’s good for a child to grow up. No one should get things before it’s time. I’ve seen so many comedians crash because they get that stuff early. I’m glad that I went through the stuff that I went through, because when I did get famous, I knew how to handle it. I don’t think I would have been that way at 19. Oh, God, the scandals! I would have fucked everybody. I’m serious. Industry observers note that what’s your advice to people who want to get into comedy or entertainment? Don’t look at the now. Look at the how. I didn’t just pop up. There’s no such thing as an overnight success, and there’s no such thing as sacrificing everything so you can make it. If you’re trying to make it, still get a job, pay your fucking rent, pay your fucking taxes, get some goddamn health insurance, live a regular life. Don’t be a starving artist — there’s no fucking such thing. And whatever craft that you’re going into, you are not better than that craft. That craft has been there way before you, and it will be there way after you’re dead. So, don’t think that you’re better than the craft of comedy. Bow to the craft.

It has been revealed that you’re no stranger to mixing comedy and politics. What are your thoughts on America’s current political moment? I want everybody to understand that the reason that we have so much hate right now is because we don’t have love for ourselves individually. You can’t give something that you don’t have. I know that sounds like a cliché, but you have to start loving yourself. Every part — your insecurities, your badness, your mistakes, your flaws, your wonderfulness, all of that. The only way we’re gonna beat all of this hate is if everyone starts having a full, solid love for themselves. Because when you love yourself and actually like yourself, you don’t want to hurt nobody. And then you will get your ass up and go vote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta employees have expressed concerns about what appear to be major privacy breaches when using Muse, at the moment the second most popular free iPhone app in the App Store with over 10 million downloads.

This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user ….

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was introduced the same month, with the tech giant describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”.

Recent findings suggest that muse initially launched as an iPhone app, with Mac and iPad apps following shortly afterwards. It immediately moved to the top of the US App Store charts, overtaking ChatGPT. It quickly exceeded 5 million downloads following a major advertising push by Meta, and that number has since doubled.

Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t long before major privacy concerns were raised. Tech writer Jason Aten reported that the Mac app accessed his messages despite him explicitly refusing permission. The app then lied to him about how it had achieved this. Meta described this as a bug.

Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts, directing them instead to their own server.

I said at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report.

According to recent reports, reuters now reports Meta employees discussing further breaches. This includes another example of accessing encrypted messages without permission.

An employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp.

In a recent development, “This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post.

In a recent development, the report says this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission.

Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”.

Sources indicate that “I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information. Update: Meta has now told us that the balances were definitely hallucinations.

Recent findings suggest that "AI Agent" = Malware. There are an expanding number of "I told it not to do that" cases.

Recent findings suggest that the instructions (prompt) you give the agent are a tiny fraction of the total prompt context the agent uses, and Meta/Grok/etc. is not going to let you see that context. Agents harvesting your data (ex. see full disk access) and sending it to the mothership is just another revenue/training stream. Even if you are paying you are still the product.

Meta has taken matter with the messaging claims. It states that access to either notifications or messaging must be explicitly granted.

With Android, people have the option to grant apps notification access, which allows apps to see notifications as they’re received. This is something users need to opt in to and is not specific to Muse. With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on.

The company also implies that the experience of employees may relate to internal versions of Muse.

Employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.

I can only repeat my previous take on Muse: Nope.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that “I write behind the wheel of the van,” Jason Scott, leader of the namesake band Jason Scott and the High Heat, says. “There’s no other time.”.

Bassist Ryan Magnani, however, calls bullshit: The van is just one of the places that Scott, a prolific Oklahoma writer, is able to come up with material. “Just the other day, you came off of a drive and you remarked, ‘I think I just wrote a cool song.’ And I am looking around like, ‘Where did you write a song? You don’t have a guitar,’” Magnani claims. ‘You said, ‘Nah, I was just thinking about it.’”.

Jason Scott and the High Heat released their latest album Play Boy back in September, marking their second record on the Leo33 label and their second in just over a year, following the March 2025 drop of American Grin. Scott has spent the better part of a decade writing songs shaped by his Pentecostal upbringing and the personal and artistic awakenings he had after pursuing music full-time, but Play Boy goes hard in a different direction. It’s best described as “Jason Scott, unfiltered,” a collection of songs written on whims.

“It has no inherent meaning, and it did not come from anywhere,” Scott claims, “other than, ‘That’s all we be doin’ out here.’”.

Sources indicate that with Scott on guitar and vocals and Magnani on bass, the High Heat features Gabriel Mor on guitar, Garrison Brown on guitar and keys, and Tremaine “Bobby” Wade on drums. Taylor Johnson, a one-time member, is the band’s producer. On this particular afternoon, they are gathered around a table at an Irish pub on Manhattan’s Upper West Side, coming in hot from a European run and gearing up for a CBS Saturday Morning taping the next day. Together, the High Heat are a group of misfits from Oklahoma capable of being sincere in one moment, and irreverent in the next.

The group skewed toward the latter when they introduced Play Boy to the world in early summer by releasing the twangy “Shit Show” and its accompanying video. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

If the song plays out as something of a parody of A-list entertainers (“Come and get it, either pass that shit or hit it/They is until they isn’t, honey that’s the biz,” is the song’s hook), the video is a fever dream. Brett Loudermilk and Zain Curtis of Paperboy Studios, best-known for Ke$ha’s NSFW “Boy Crazy” video, oversaw the production, which opens with the band in a living room, nursing severe hangovers, before a parade of increasingly-absurd characters wanders in. Midway through, the room becomes the site of a burlesque show. Wade is walked on a leash by a dominatrix.

According to recent reports, the band indicates the shoot itself followed the theme in the video, of starting out tame and building to chaos, as the day went on. “They didn’t tell us what they were gonna do. They just kept surprising us,” Mor says. “They’d say, ‘We’ve got a woman, and she’s gonna walk Bob like a dog.’ Every scene was like, ‘We have no idea what’s gonna happen.’”.

The album cover features a pregnant woman modeling lingerie and holding a cigarette in front of a dressing room mirror, with a table littered with half-drank cups of liquor nearby.

“That was Grace, and it was the first time we had met her,” Scott states. “She did such an incredible job on the shoot, and we ended up with all these cool photos of her. One just worked out to be our artwork. She has had baby June since then.”.

Recent findings suggest that since “Shit Show,” the High Heat have gotten even more conceptual with their music videos.” The latest, “How to Get Away With Murder,” pokes deadly fun at dating in the digital age. It’s cinematic, haunting, and very bloody. Making such adventurous, boundary-pushing videos is only adding to the respect they have already earned from their peers, and Scott and his bandmates wield influence across Americana music. Mor has served as the stylist for Flatland Cavalry. Magnani has directed videos for Wyatt Flores. Scott himself played the lead character in Jason Isbell’s “King of Oklahoma” video.

So, when it came time to record Play Boy, the High Heat found plenty of willing collaborators. “Shit Show” alone featured background vocals by Ken Pomeroy — recently named Emerging Artist of the Year at the Americana Honors & Awards — and keys by fellow Oklahoman John Fullbright. Rod Elkins, drummer for Tyler Childers and the Food Stamps, played on the track.

“We just ask the cool people that we know,” Brown notes of the guest appearances.

Even before Play Boy, the High Heat were edging closer to being the cool people that other artists know. Their schedule includes high-profile festival stops at January’s Mile 0 Fest and their Stagecoach debut next spring in Indio, California. They’re also working on prepares for their annual Loser’s Ball concert, slated for the holiday season in Oklahoma City. Their live show, much like their album interview in a Newly introduced York pub, is loose and aimed at giving fans the chance to leave the show with a memory.   • Canva today revealed fresh controls that will let Free and Pro users choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in light of growing pushback from customers who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing fresh settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content. Here are the details.

Canva today revealed fresh controls that will let Free and Pro users choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.

The organization notes that both controls are available at no additional cost and can be turned on or off at any time.

According to Canva, “the future of creativity isn’t a choice between AI and no AI.” For this reason, it is introducing the following controls:.

The company says that, while it knows that there is an ongoing debate between consumers with opposing views on whether AI has a place in creative work, it thinks “both views are valid”:.

“It’s not our place to tell anyone how to create, so today we’re launching two upcoming controls that put that decision firmly with our community […].”.

Importantly, the organization noted that select features that use AI without generating upcoming content will remain available even when generative AI features are turned off:.

In a recent development, “Some of Canva’s everyday editing tools use AI to make simple tasks faster, without generating anything newly introduced. Background Remover, one of Canva’s most popular tools, lifts a subject cleanly out of a photo in a single click, and Magic Grab lets creators select an object in an image and move it somewhere else in the design. Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design.”.

Canva added that these tools also won’t add an AI label to a design’s metadata, since that label is reserved for AI-generated content.

As for the firm’s design content library, Canva remarked that while “a small portion of the library is AI-generated content made by Canva, including some abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics,” its community has told it “they want an easier way to find design assets made by real people, so the content control reduces the number of AI-generated templates and elements that appear in search results and recommendations.”.

With today’s announcement, Canva is essentially expanding on the AI permissions already available to administrators of Business, Enterprise, Teams, and Education accounts, which let organizations control how their teams use AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 13-years-in-the-making Grand Theft Auto VI has been hailed for its of-the-moment touches, but it does have one quaintly anachronistic aspect: Nobody reaches for the aux. The game’s in-universe radio stations provide the soundtrack to its criminal and romantic endeavors, with drivers eschewing streaming and flipping the dial until they find their favorites. Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, appropriately, feels like a frantic flip through a dial so wide, it can even fit a still-trucking smooth jazz station.

It has been revealed that opening track “Starting From Zero,” a collaboration between the aggro-electro duo Justice (who composed the game’s score) and soul crooner Michael McDonald, transports the listener to the sublime, the combination of thudding synths and McDonald’s immediately identifiable voice throwing back to the days of hits being launched from buddy-cop movies and Miami Vice. It’s pastiche, sure, but it’s pastiche done well, and it bookends nicely with the album’s closing cut. “Overtown Lights,” a collaboration between Return to Forever bassist Stanley Clarke, pianist and bandleader Robert Glasper, and drummer Yussef Dayes, evokes a carefree late-night drive over streets slicked with rain and illuminated by reflected headlights.

If Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album were just a collection of homages to the good-ish old days of neon t-shirts paired with blazers, it would probably be a solid listen, as evidenced by the genre-splicing Justice-SZA-King Gizzard-Tame Impala team-up “Flower In A Hurricane” and the training-montage-ready Dua Lipa cut “Go Easy.” But this collection is more than that — similar to the game, whose intricate details firmly place it in a heightened version of the present, it’s a wide-ranging representation of popular music’s current moment. “That’s It,” the collaboration between Swedish MC Yung Lean, Atlanta kingpin Future, and superproducer Metro Boomin, follows the Justice/McDonald collab, and even though it opens with icy synths that feel connected to the previous track, the fluttering trap snares and bone-rattling bass, as well as Lean’s anxiety-ridden lyrics, jolt the milieu back to 2026. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Industry observers note that hip-hop’s 21st-century vanguard is well-represented on GTAVI:TA, with rap enigma Travis Scott’s spaced-out “RHYNO” — produced by Daft Punk’s Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo — and the frantic Kodak Black/Don Toliver collaboration “Let’s Rock” heading a pack that also includes Playboi Carti, Cardi B, and Young Thug. Music from pop’s Spanish-speaking diaspora is also in ample supply; regional Mexican stars Fuerza Regida’s thumping “Suzuki” is a throwdown, and “Largate,” the collaboration between singer-songwriter Helado Negro and dreampop romantic Kali Uchis, is one of the album’s true highlights, the singers ruminating on a breakup in the midst of a haze conjured by strummed guitars. Trending Stories Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake Princess of Wales Reflects on Cancer Battle in 'Heal' Documentary Special The Making of My Chemical Romance's 'The Black Parade'.

GTAVI:TA’s pop universe operates on hyperspeed, with BLACKPINK’s JENNIE’s voice welding itself to the robot-rocking synths of “Power Trip,”  Zara Larsson paying homage to her fellow Swedes Ace Of Base on the sinuous “Fast Emotion,” and Camila Cabello finding a middle ground between her full-speed-ahead c, xoxo era and her more mellow cuts like “Havana.” (Not having a Latin freestyle-nodding selection accompany a game that’s so Floridian seems wrong, but there’s always GTAVII.).

According to recent reports, A couple of tracks hold their own, genre-wise: Irascible Nashville star Morgan Wallen’s “Last Thing You Need” rides in on a candy-coated guitar riff and splits the difference between the Urban Cowboy era and the present moment; Keith Richards lays down a faithful version of Jimmy Reed’s Chicago blues classic “Bright Lights, Big City”; and The Time’s Jesse Johnson teams up with torch-carrying producer Dam-Funk for “Stone Kold Krazy Luuv,” a slow jam that brings together sparkling synths, flinty riffing, and a thick bassline. These songs not only feel like the results of serendipitous dial spins; along with the rest of GTAVI:TA, they nod to the parent album’s status as one of monoculture’s last blockbusters.

Latest Update: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • Sources indicate that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

Sources indicate that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

Sources indicate that A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

It has been revealed that in the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn rapidly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

In a recent development, during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

Sources indicate that an image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

It has been revealed that he insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

It has been revealed that on the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most notable processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

Industry observers note that that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very promptly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she claims, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, introduced in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

Sources indicate that when Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

Recent findings suggest that the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller indicates. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

Industry observers note that the teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

Sources indicate that but duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

Recent findings suggest that “Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

Recent findings suggest that if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

Industry observers note that on the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

According to recent reports, but even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” notes Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

Recent findings suggest that as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Sources indicate that twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Sources indicate that among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller indicates with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

Industry observers note that for example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

Recent findings suggest that with just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as swiftly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

According to recent reports, “The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller indicates. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller notes.

According to recent reports, who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I n December, Gustavo Dudamel will make his much-anticipated return to conduct the Los Angeles Philharmonic for a string of dates. It’s the first time he will head back to his former home of nearly 20 years since beginning his tenure as the Upcoming York Philharmonic’s Music and Artistic Director. Given the multiple standing ovations and chants of “Gustavo” that resonated through the Hollywood Bowl during his final LA Phil bow in late August, his arrival will be a much welcome one.

Alongside his trip back to the West Coast, Rolling Stone can exclusively announce a documentary about Dudamel and the LA Phil will premiere on Dec. 7 coinciding with his concerts at Walt Disney Hall on Dec. 4, 5, and 6. The documentary, titled Symphony of a Thousand, is described as “Set during challenging times in L.A., the film encapsulates Dudamel’s philosophy on how music can create connection and community in an increasingly fractured world.”.

The Jennifer Tiexiera-directed film, produced by Brad Pitt’s Blueprint B Entertainment, features footage from Dudamel and the LA Phil’s pair of performances at 2025’s Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival, where they made history as the first major orchestra to perform a full set at the massive event. It features Dave Grohl,  LL Cool J, Cynthia Erivo, Natasha Bedingfield, Becky G, CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, and Zedd. Kevin Macdonald serves as the executive producer, with producers Jeremy Kleiner, Dede Gardner, and Chloe Mamelok.

In a recent development, landmark pop culture moments like this have peppered the course of Dudamel’s trailblazing career. And he wasn’t about to go (east) quietly. His final nights helming the LA Phil culminated in a weekend at the Bowl that featured the Foo Fighters and other pop luminaries, concerts that doubled as a benefit for his home country of Venezuela. A conversation at the Grammy Museum followed.

“I met Gustavo at a party about 12 years ago, and I fell in love with him. As a heterosexual man, it confused me,” Coldplay’s Chris Martin affectionately jokes when joining Dudamel and LA Phil onstage during the benefit concert for Venezuela finale. “And I realized it wasn’t so much sexual as musical in the way I just wanted to cuddle him forever. And we’ve been musically cuddling ever since.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Trailing Dudamel during his final full-time week in L.A., that sentiment carries through to every interaction. At the closed final rehearsal on a Sunday morning in August, camera crews swirl around as two women busily work to notate the score, and a handful of onlookers from the team at the Bowl gather to take in the moment in the blazing heat. There’s a hushed reverence knowing an era is coming to an end, but also smiles abound, particularly from Dudamel who warmly hugs old friends as they join him onstage.

Industry observers note that as he conducts, he throws the full weight of his body in a stance both graceful and animated — like a kid at his first dance. His baton alights in the air and comes down, and the orchestra responds, while he swoops and sways to the music. “5/4 pum pum,” Dudamel instructs as they run through one composition. Later, Meme del Real from Café Tacvba takes the stage to rehearse the poignant “Eras.” Lasso follows with an a cappella of “En Otra Vida.”.

According to recent reports, it’s the morning after their phenomenal performance with Foo Fighters, which marked the band’s first-ever set at the Hollywood Bowl. That pairing is not an unusual one for Dudamel, though. He’s made a name for himself breaking down perceived traditional genre boundaries in his 17 years at the Bowl, where he’s collaborated with an array of artists, including LL Cool J, Christina Aguilera, and Beck, who later at the finale concert performs “Ride Lonesome.” Beck’s dad, celebrated arranger-composer David Campbell, also attends the final rehearsal. In a recent development, “If I reflect about how I feel, yes, I feel exhausted,” Dudamel tells Rolling Stone with a smile when we meet at the Grammy Museum a couple of days later. “Every day a rehearsal, every day a concert. Next day a different program, another concert.” It’s been a nonstop whirlwind, but it’s also been a time “full of beauty,” he says.

“I have the chance to dive inside of all of that amount of talent — because it’s not only the soloists that play with me; it’s all that orchestra, that 100 musicians that are there, that I have shared 17 years of my life with them, and of course it doesn’t finish,” he continues. “This goes to eternity because when you develop something that is so deep and so powerful as developing an identity through music, it’s the biggest privilege … Every single note, every single second that I have the chance to share, or people share with me, that is a privilege to have the chance to work with all of these people and to create all of this environment.”.

Sources indicate that if there are a couple of overarching words to describe Dudamel, they would be magnetic charm. When we arrive at the Grammy Museum a few hours before his event, several people rush him to ask for selfies, to which he happily obliges before he’s quickly ushered into the building. People from the music world and beyond appear drawn to him, not only for the music he helms and the open environment he’s created around it, but also for his altruism.

It has been revealed that at intermission during Dudamel’s Hollywood Bowl finale, Coldplay’s Martin heads backstage to rehearse with YOLA, the youth orchestra inspired by Dudamel’s own experience coming up in El Sistema, the publicly-funded National Network of Youth and Children Orchestras of Venezuela. (It was there while discovering music technique that “I saw the immense and infinite possibilities of all kinds of music,” Dudamel says.) Martin asks each child their name before leading them through a warm-up and taking to the piano. He vamps his lyrics to “Viva La Vida” before the choir comes in with the buoyant Oh-oh-oh bridge. “Absolutely fantastic,” Martin tells the students. He reminds them: “Remember when we’re out there onstage, this is our band … We’re doing this together.” Later onstage, they deliver their spine-tingly performance, which prompts a crowd-wide sing-along.

YOLA, which provides free instruments and education to create social change through music, is a vital part of Dudamel’s legacy and his north star. “I grew up not in an environment of conservatory, rigid. No,” he says. “It was music as a tool of social transformation — that is El Sistema. And of course, for me, opening spaces for young people to have access to music as a tool for them to have beauty, to have creativity, to have empathy, creating together — that is for me the most important thing. And [as] artistic institutions, we have to do that … for people to see the transforming power of music.

“When you have this chance to transform your life, creating harmony, creating beauty together — when you go out as a citizen, you behave differently because you see the real dimension of connection that goes beyond any material thing, any ideological point of view, and then you are connected through the empathy of human being and doing things beautiful for others.”.

Sources indicate that as for his hopes to bring a similar program to Newly introduced York and beyond, he believes it’s imperative. “We don’t have the chance in this world to contemplate, to really see each other, to create something that requires discipline, but at the same time joy together. When you are doing music, in an orchestra, in a choir, and you feel that first moment that you create harmony and that you are part of something beautiful and powerful, that enhances your spirit. I think that is the way for our kids to be inspired, especially in the chaotic but beautiful, in the only world that we have. So we have to create more spaces like this.”.

In a recent development, as a longtime champion of crossover collaborations, Dudamel attracts artists across genres and disciplines, but a recent team-up came by way of an unusual source, via actor Bradley Cooper, who is a mutual friend of Dudamel’s and Stella Hopkins. Hopkins began sharing scores with Dudamel, which were composed by her husband, actor Anthony Hopkins. It led to them working on an album.

It has been revealed that “The thing about musicians is that they, unlike actors, they don’t have that ego,” Anthony Hopkins tells Rolling Stone of working with Dudamel. The pair met up at the Grammy Museum to talk about their collaboration on Hopkins’ debut classical album, Life Is a Dream. Dudamel conducted London’s Philharmonia Orchestra for the project, which comprises work Hopkins has composed over the course of more than six decades.

During his Venezuelan benefit show, Dudamel and LA Phil performed Hopkins’ “Stella Aria,” a moving ode to the actor’s wife, which featured a beautiful solo from Venezuelan cellist Gregorio Nieto at the concert.

“It is a great honor and a privilege because he actually endorsed my music,” states Hopkins. “I mean, I’m always filled with self-doubts as we all are … I have no theoretical, technical, musical training as such — everything is instinctive from childhood. So, naturally in me is the — ‘do I, is this good enough?,’ But when I sat there and Gustavo got up onto the podium to conduct the massive orchestra there, and I was astounded as the sound came out. He’s playing my music. Did I write that?’”.

Dudamel has a knack for making artists feel comfortable in new situations as his next act in New York illustrates — it has begun, unsurprisingly, with rave reviews. In September, his premiere debut with the New York Philharmonic at Radio City Music Hall drew the kind of rock star lineup one would expect from Dudamel. Hosted by Liev Schreiber, it featured Lizzo, St. Vincent, and Joaquina. “The Philharmonic plays for Dudamel with visible investment and enthusiasm,” a New York Times review of his first week’s New York concerts reads. “Its members haven’t looked this happy onstage in years. Either he inspires them, or his starry arrival has lifted their morale. Or both. It’s apparent his inclusive approach to music uplifts both musicians and fans alike. And it is contagious. His Radio City Music Hall opener began with a standing ovation.

It has been revealed that “That is one thing that I love the most. You know, to really make people see that there are no borders between us — we enjoy, we can be there, we can be listening,” he says of his approach. “When you really listen not only with your ears, but with your soul, the music becomes a dimension that is infinite.”.

Latest Update: UK court rules Apple can share the top secret order everyone already knew

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.
  • Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the issue ….
  • The story centers on Apple’s introduction of the Advanced Data Protection (ADP) privacy feature back in 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.

Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the issue ….

The story centers on Apple’s introduction of the Advanced Data Protection (ADP) privacy feature back in 2022. This extended end-to-end encryption to almost all your iCloud data, meaning Apple has no access, and therefore cannot grant access to any government agencies who come knocking on its door.

Industry observers note that the feature is off by default because it means Apple cannot help you access any of your data if, for example, you forget your iCloud password. However, those who want to maximize the privacy of their iCloud account can enable it.

In 2025, the British government ordered Apple to create a backdoor to allow access by security services and law enforcement. Even worse, the order was issued under legislation that prohibits companies from revealing that they have received this demand.

It has been revealed that this would have meant that British customers who enabled ADP would think that their data was safe when in fact it wasn’t. As we’ve remarked many times before, any backdoor created for use by the good guys is vulnerable to discovery and exploitation by the bad guys.

It would have been illegal for Apple to reveal that it had been instructed to compromise the privacy of customer data, but the company found a clever way to effectively communicate this without breaking the law. Apple announced it was withdrawing ADP from the UK without explaining its reason.

“Apple can no longer offer Advanced Data Protection (ADP) in the United Kingdom to latest owners and current UK users will eventually need to disable this security feature. ADP protects iCloud data with end-to-end encryption, which means the data can only be decrypted by the user who owns it, and only on their trusted devices. We are gravely disappointed that the protections provided by ADP will not be available to our customers in the UK […] As we have noted many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will.”.

Tell me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP without telling me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP ….

At this point, it was an open secret. However, ridiculously, despite the fact that everyone in the security and privacy field knew about it and was talking about it, Apple was still not allowed to officially confirm it.

The iPhone maker asked the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) to allow it to openly discuss the order, with privacy campaigners backing this call. The Financial Times reports that the court has now ruled in Apple’s favor.

It has been revealed that the UK government must admit that it issued a secret order to Apple to allow it access to encrypted customer data, a court has ruled […] The Home Office has “not established that it would be damaging to national security” to reveal that Apple had received a “technical capability notice” (TCN), the tribunal stated. The ruling means that […] “much” of Apple and the non-profits’ legal challenge can now take place in open court.

One of the great ironies is that most people had never heard of ADP until the government effectively made it headline news in the tech press three years after it released – a classic example of the Streisand Effect.

It has been revealed that this ruling is a win both for transparency and commonsense. To be clear, the actual requirement for a backdoor remains in place, but this can now be challenged in open court.

Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that xc is a heterogeneous data-parallel language.
  • This repository holds the compiler, its GUI framework and the tools and applications built with them.
  • It is one repository, but it is worked on as several separate streams, and each stream stays inside its own tree.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that xc is a heterogeneous data-parallel language. Write an ordinary loop, in xc or in C, and xcc runs it across every CPU core, on the GPU through Metal, CUDA, Vulkan or WebGPU, across several GPUs from different vendors at once, or on a GPU on another machine, and keeps whichever is fastest. The kernels are generated by xcc itself and carried in the executable, so a build needs no GPU toolkit. Documentation, benchmarks and downloads are at https://compile-xc.org.

This repository holds the compiler, its GUI framework and the tools and applications built with them.

It is one repository, but it is worked on as several separate streams, and each stream stays inside its own tree.

Two rules keep the streams' work apart:.

Pull requests, from outside contributors and from the streams alike, keep main always gated:.

According to recent reports, private/ is not part of the repository. It is ignored by git and holds the working rules, the notes on open and fixed bugs, and other material that is never published. Nothing under it is ever committed.

Build and install the compiler first (see compiler/USAGE.md), then build whichever other tree you are working in against it.

Recent findings suggest that settings that depend on your machines, such as the Linux test host or the location of the GEM desktop sources, live in build.env at the repository root. Copy build.env.template to build.env and fill in the values you need. build.env is ignored by git. A variable left empty turns off the step that needs it.

Sources indicate that pull requests are welcome. CONTRIBUTING.md claims how a change gets into main: the contributor licence agreement you sign once, where changes go, and how to build and test with an installed release. Everyone taking part agrees to the code of conduct. Security problems are reported privately, as SECURITY.md describes.

Recent findings suggest that every benchmark figure on the site is measured on hardware the project has bought, and the machines that matter most for data-parallel work are expensive. A loan or donation goes straight into the compiler: a back end and a runtime tuned on the device, kept working by being tested on it every release, and its figures published beside the others. We would most like:.

If you make or sell hardware like this and would like xc to run well on it, write to xc@oobergeek.net.

My apologies but I wasn't great at keeping private details out of the ~3000 or so checkins made to get this far, and the thought of going back and changing everything didn't really appeal. So, clean start, and I'll be more diligent from now on...

#108463. What China Gets From Its AI Honeypots and Smuggled Chips

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1271 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollingstone ↗ Open Full Page

What China Gets From Its AI Honeypots and Smuggled Chips

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1271 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollingstone

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You could start casting the movie right now: Jensen Huang, the Taiwanese-American CEO of Nvidia, the most vital tech company in the world, is sucked into an illicit affair with a Chinese spy.
  • At least, that’s the simple version of the story.
  • Broadly speaking, there are two ways to think about AI, says Kyle Chan, an expert on Chinese technology development at the Brookings Institution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You could start casting the movie right now: Jensen Huang, the Taiwanese-American CEO of Nvidia, the most vital tech company in the world, is sucked into an illicit affair with a Chinese spy. The most valuable tech in the world — Huang’s super-powered computer chips — are smuggled into China or installed into data centers connected to America’s greatest rival. Above it all, the possibility of a super-intelligent AI, a true artificial mind, looms — and its creator will be positioned to rule the world.

At least, that’s the simple version of the story. But the real picture of the great geopolitical AI race is both more complex and more unbelievable than the tale of spies and smuggling that’s playing out in the press right now. China wants the U.S.’s chips — that much is clear. But why? And what can our only real rival power actually do with them? To answer this, Rolling Stone spoke with two experts in the Chinese tech sector, who pulled back the curtain on what the superpower actually wants when it comes to AI — and why it’s willing to use sex, smuggling and lies to get there.

Broadly speaking, there are two ways to think about AI, says Kyle Chan, an expert on Chinese technology development at the Brookings Institution.

Recent findings suggest that the first is as a straight race to one goal: creating a truly intelligent AI that surpasses human intelligence in all general tasks and can improve itself autonomously. In the industry, this is known as AGI, or Artificial General Intelligence. This point of view holds that the first country or firm to achieve true AGI will have an earth-shattering advantage over any competition in economics, war, medicine, and technology. Basically, it sets the world of AI up as a winner-take-all race. Many U.S. officials — including, at times, Trump himself — have made this argument, alongside many of the private sector CEOs actually working on the technology.

Sources indicate that “If you start with that assumption, then the effort to slow down China is nearly existential,” Chan says. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

The biggest advantage the U.S. has is Nvidia’s chips. The most powerful computer chips in the world are made by one facility in Taiwan, using incredibly complex and rare machines manufactured by one company in the Netherlands. It is a process so detailed and scientifically complex that it might as well be magic. Other companies can make chips, of course, but none of them can make chips as well as the single manufacturing company in Taiwan that Nvidia and most of the U.S. tech giants use. AI companies need these chips, and these chips alone, to run the most advanced AI models — which is why the U.S. has done a lot to limit China’s access to them, setting export controls on who Nvidia can sell their chips to and which countries they can be shipped into.

Because of this constraint, the Chinese don’t really see AI the same way as most of the U.S. industry does.

Instead of an existential threat, Chan says, the second way to look at AI is a very powerful technology that will not necessarily lead to some massive strategic advantage for the first team past the AGI post. That makes the AI race a longer-term game, decided more by which power can holistically incorporate the advances of super-computing into its society and economy, which China has largely focused on doing.

Sources indicate that “What we’re kind of seeing unfold in the future is two different markets,” remarked Kenton Thibaut, a China expert at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. The U.S. is focused on “frontier” systems — the absolute cutting-edge AI, powered by their chip advantage — while China is supplying “near frontier” technology that hits different parts of the market for AI technology. In China, Thibaut said, AI is viewed as a “general purpose” technology that should be harnessed for practical use as rapidly as possible, rather than a more conceptual race to the furthest frontier. Related Content Man Found Guilty of Igniting Blaze That Became the Devastating Palisades Fire Trump Says He ‘Can’t Speak To’ Whether Russia is a Friend to America Trump Got Played by Putin and Xi Your Favorite THC Drinks Are About to Be Illegal.

“All of the [Chinese] policies and major policy pronouncements and planning around AI have to do with ‘How do we make this useful in society?’” Thibaut remarked. “I haven’t seen anything like that in the US.”.

Recent findings suggest that “[China’s] version of winning is being able to benefit the most from AI,” Chan says. “Integrate it in their economy, automate their factories, speed up drug discovery, et cetera. [They want it to] help them win across all these other domains, rather than this singular focus on achieving AGI.”.

According to recent reports, it’s a philosophical difference that is fueled by the physical constraints that the Chinese tech sector faces. The U.S. has access to more computing power than any other nation, allowing them to push the envelope. Companies like Anthropic have asked the U.S. government to regulate them more, fearful that their AI models will run out of control. In China, these discussions are scarce, Thibaut notes, because the hardware they’re working with basically makes them moot — and the Chinese government is predisposed to prevent any societal disruptions. Instead, Chinese AI firms are usually focused on doing more with less — creating working, practical products and applications of AI that get the most out of whatever computing power they can harness.

And in some cases, that’s where the spies come in. The Nvidia honeypot scandal was largely controversial because it included a woman who ran a Singaporean front manufacturer that set up data centers in Southeast Asia stocked with Taiwan-made super-chips, and then leased the use of those chips to Chinese companies. Chan refers to this loophole, and the broader Chinese project of getting their hands on American tech, as a “bridge” to the country’s real goal: separating themselves from the Western “tech stack,” while still retaining competitive computing power. Eventually, Chan states, China wants to have its own version of the super-manufacturers in Taiwan, its own version of the very best chips — but until then, it has to use more subtle methods to get what it wants.

“If they want to keep pace today, they do still need access to Nvidia chips now,” Chan notes. Trending Stories Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake Princess of Wales Reflects on Cancer Battle in 'Heal' Documentary Special The Making of My Chemical Romance's 'The Black Parade'.

Some parts of the U.S. government may be helping them achieve that. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnik had been very lax with Nvidia and Huang personally, allowing the tech giant to continue selling to companies that the U.S. knew were linked with China. While Trump has said he views AI as a winner-take-all race, Reuters reported that his administration also signed off on the sale of 900,000 AI chips to Chinese companies in one six-month period, and his own AI Czar David Sacks has explicitly advocated for selling more chips directly to China.

China, then, has allies to go along with its spies — and it seems that one way or another, it’s getting all the chips it needs.
